      <content name="title"><span class="qt1">Psoriatic</span> <span class="qt0">Arthritis</span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p><span class="qt1">Psoriasis</span> is a skin disease that causes itchy or sore patches of thick, red skin with silvery scales. You usually get them on your elbows, knees, scalp, back, face, palms and feet, but they can show up on other parts of your body.</p><p>Some people with <span class="qt1">psoriasis have psoriatic</span> <span class="qt0">arthritis</span>.  It causes pain, stiffness, and swelling of the joints.  It is often mild, but can sometimes be serious and affect many joints. The joint and skin problems don't always happen at the same time.</p><p>Your doctor will do a physical exam and imaging tests to diagnose <span class="qt1">psoriatic</span> <span class="qt0">arthritis</span>. There is no cure, but medicines can help control inflammation and pain. In rare cases, you might need surgery to repair or replace damaged joints.</p></content>

      <content name="title"><span class="qt1">Psoriasis</span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p><span class="qt1">Psoriasis</span> is a skin disease that causes itchy or sore patches of thick, red skin with silvery scales. You usually get the patches on your elbows, knees, scalp, back, face, palms and feet, but they can show up on other parts of your body.  Some people who have <span class="qt1">psoriasis</span> also get a form of <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> called <span class="qt1">psoriatic</span> <span class="qt0">arthritis</span>.</p><p>A problem with your immune system causes <span class="qt1">psoriasis</span>. In a process called cell turnover, skin cells that grow deep in your skin rise to the surface. Normally, this takes a month. In <span class="qt1">psoriasis</span>, it happens in just days because your cells rise too fast. </p><p><span class="qt1">Psoriasis</span> can be hard to diagnose because it can look like other skin diseases. Your doctor might need to look at a small skin sample under a microscope.</p><p><span class="qt1">Psoriasis</span> can last a long time, even a lifetime. Symptoms come and go. Things that make them worse include:</p><ul><li>Infections</li><li>Stress</li><li>Dry skin</li><li>Certain medicines</li></ul><p><span class="qt1">Psoriasis</span> usually occurs in adults. It sometimes runs in families. Treatments include creams, medicines, and light therapy.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of <span class="qt0">Arthritis</span> and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases </p></content>

    <document rank="2" url="https://medlineplus.gov/arthritis.html">
      <content name="title"><span class="qt0">Arthritis</span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Joint inflammation</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is <span class="qt0">arthritis</span>?<p>If you feel pain and stiffness in your body or have trouble moving around, you might have <span class="qt0">arthritis</span>. Any disorder that affects the joints is often called <span class="qt0">arthritis</span>. Joints are places where two bones meet, such as your elbow or knee.</p><p>Most types of <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> can cause joint pain and inflammation (swelling). Over time, a swollen joint can become severely damaged. Some kinds of <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> can also cause problems in your organs, such as your eyes or skin. Treatment will depend on the type of <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> you have.</p>What are the types of <span class="qt0">arthritis</span>?<p>Common types of <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> include:</p><ul><li><span class="qt0">Osteoarthritis</span> is the most common type of <span class="qt0">arthritis</span>. It's often related to aging or injury.</li><li>Autoimmune <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> happens when your body's immune system attacks healthy cells in your body by mistake.  Rheumatoid <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> is the most common form of this type of <span class="qt0">arthritis</span>.</li><li>Juvenile <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> is a type of <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> that happens in children.</li><li>Infectious <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> is an infection that has spread from another part of your body to the joint. Reactive <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> is one type.</li><li><span class="qt1">Psoriatic</span> <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> affects people with <span class="qt1">psoriasis</span> (itchy or sore scaly red and white skin patches).</li><li>Gout is a painful type of <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> that happens when too much uric acid builds up in your body. It often starts in the big toe. Other joints can also be affected.</li><li>Ankylosing spondylitis is a type of <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> of the spine that can cause stiffness and make it difficult to move and bend.</li></ul>What are the symptoms of <span class="qt0">arthritis</span>?<p>Pain, redness, warmth, and joint inflammation are common <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> symptoms. You may not be able to move your joint as well as it should. Other symptoms could include fever, weight loss, breathing difficulties, or a rash.</p><p>Symptoms often get worse as you age. Some symptoms of <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> may be signs of other illnesses.</p>Who is more likely to get <span class="qt0">arthritis</span>?<p>A few things that might increase your chance of getting <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> include:</p><ul><li>Family history. You may be more likely to get certain types of <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> if a member of your family has the disorder.</li><li>Age. The risk of getting many types of <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> increases with age.</li><li>Sex. Certain types of <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> are more common in women, while other types are more common in men.</li></ul><p>Other factors that might increase your risk of getting <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> include having a previous joint injury, obesity, or lupus.</p>How is <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> diagnosed?<p>To find out if you have <span class="qt0">arthritis</span>, your health care provider may:</p><ul><li>Ask you about your medical history, including your symptoms.</li><li>Do a physical exam.</li><li>Order blood tests or take x-rays.</li></ul><p>Your provider may refer you to a rheumatologist (a doctor who specializes in <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> care) for tests, diagnosis, and care.</p>What are the treatments for <span class="qt0">arthritis</span>?<p>Treatment depends on the type of <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> you have. It may include medicine or surgery. Your provider will work with you to improve your symptoms and quality of life.</p><p>A few ways to help manage your symptoms include:</p><ul><li>Hot or cold packs</li><li>Relaxation techniques</li><li>Use of splints, braces, and/or assistive devices</li></ul><p>NIH: National Institute of <span class="qt0">Arthritis</span> and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases</p></content>
